content.overview: Administrative tribunals grew to provide specialised, speedy and accessible adjudication in areas where ordinary courts faced volume, technicality or delay. Their growth reflects the expansion of the administrative state and the need for expert dispute resolution under statute.
content.glance: Explain the pressures (volume, expertise, speed, cost) that drove tribunal growth; note constitutional limits from judicial review and independence requirements.
content.study: The proliferation of regulatory and welfare legislation generated disputes unsuited to exclusively ordinary-court resolution. Tribunals offered specialised fact-finding, informal procedure and speed. Growth raised concerns about independence, appeal structure and exclusion of High Court jurisdiction — concerns addressed in leading decisions on tribunal design. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Constitution and parent tribunal statutes. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Reasons for Growth
sections.body: Volume of disputes; technical subject-matter; speed and cost; administrative expertise.

sections.heading: Statutory Design
sections.body: Parent statutes create tribunals with defined jurisdiction and procedure.

sections.heading: Concerns
sections.body: Independence from the executive; quality of adjudication; ouster of ordinary courts.

sections.heading: Constitutional Response
sections.body: Judicial review and structural requirements protect core judicial values.

sections.heading: Contemporary Position
sections.body: Tribunals remain essential but must meet independence and review standards.

examples.title: Volume and expertise
examples.body: A high volume of technical service disputes is channelled to a specialised tribunal. Growth is explained by expertise and speed, subject to independence and review.

examples.title: Ouster concern
examples.body: A statute seeks to exclude all High Court review of tribunal decisions. Constitutional response preserves core judicial review.

hypotheticals.question: Do tribunals exist only to bypass the courts?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. They address volume and expertise needs within constitutional limits.

hypotheticals.question: Does tribunal growth abolish High Court jurisdiction?
hypotheticals.analysis: Core judicial review jurisdiction cannot be ousted.

distinctions.title: Tribunal adjudication vs ordinary court adjudication
distinctions.right: General jurisdiction, ordinary procedure, constitutional court structure

cases.name: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India
cases.facts: Constitutional position of administrative tribunals and High Court review.
cases.issue: What is the constitutional place of tribunals and judicial review by High Courts?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Tribunals may perform specialised adjudicatory functions, but decisions remain subject to High Court judicial review under Articles 226/227.
cases.holding: Tribunals upheld subject to constitutional judicial review.
cases.relevance: Leading authority already in the file.

cases.name: Union of India v Madras Bar Association
cases.issue: What institutional safeguards are required for constitutionally valid tribunals?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Tribunalisation must preserve independence, impartiality and adjudicatory standards.
cases.holding: Defective aspects of the scheme invalidated; safeguards required.

cases.name: Rojer Mathew v South Indian Bank Ltd.
cases.facts: Tribunal service and appointment rules examined.
cases.issue: Whether tribunal administration can be structured inconsistently with judicial independence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Tribunal administration must conform to constitutional requirements of independence.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a tribunals-growth problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. State reasons for growth. II. Note statutory design. III. Identify independence/review concerns. IV. Apply constitutional response.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Functional reasons; constitutional limits; authorities already in file; precise conclusion.

examTips: Cite L. Chandra Kumar for High Court review residual.
